planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens or rooted cuttings in spring once nights stay above 60°F, in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Unlike its scrambling cousins, Dwarf Allamanda holds a tidy, upright, self-branching shrub form and needs no trellis or staking.

directions: Allamanda schottii is a compact, non-vining shrub form of allamanda from Brazil, bearing the same glossy, whorled leaves and funnel-shaped golden-yellow flowers as Golden Trumpet Vine but on a naturally rounded, 2-5 foot bush rather than a sprawling vine, making it useful for foundation plantings, mixed borders, and large containers. Flowers are slightly smaller than A. cathartica, typically marked with faint reddish-brown or maroon striping in the throat, and appear in flushes from late spring through fall. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and shear lightly after each bloom flush to keep growth dense; established plants tolerate hard pruning in late winter before new growth resumes. As with all allamandas, the milky sap is toxic and irritates skin and eyes — wear gloves when pruning and keep cuttings away from children and pets. In zone 9, expect dieback after freezes with recovery from the root crown; in zone 10-11 it stays evergreen and blooms nearly year-round.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants in spring once temperatures are reliably above 60°F, in moist, fertile, very well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, fence, or arbor to support its vigorous climbing growth.

directions: 'Hendersonii' is one of the oldest and most vigorous named selections of Golden Trumpet Vine, prized for flowers that are larger and a deeper burnt-orange-gold than the species, with rounder, more overlapping petal lobes and a bronzy flush in bud. It is a stronger, ranker climber than the species type and needs a substantial structure — arbor, pergola, or chain-link fence — to carry its heavy summer-to-fall flower load. Cut back hard in late winter to control size and stimulate the new growth that carries the season's flowers, since blooms form on current-season wood. As with all allamandas, every part of the plant exudes a milky, toxic sap that irritates skin and eyes on contact; wear gloves when pruning or handling cuttings and site away from children and pets. In zone 9 it dies back hard after freezes but typically resprouts from the base; in zone 10-11 it is evergreen and flowers nearly continuously.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring once nights stay above 60°F, in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the semi-shrubby, lax habit can be left to mound and sprawl or loosely tied to a low trellis.

directions: 'Cherries Jubilee' is a striking bicolor allamanda selection whose large, funnel-shaped flowers open deep rose-red to burgundy in the throat and along the reverse of the petal lobes, fading toward a paler pink-gold face — a dramatic departure from the solid yellow of the common species and closer in spirit to the rose-purple tones of A. blanchetii. Growth is more compact and shrubbier than Golden Trumpet Vine, forming a dense, rounded mound that can be grown free-standing or lightly staked, making it well suited to large containers and mixed tropical borders. Pinch young growth to encourage branching and remove spent flower trusses to prolong the bloom season, which runs from late spring through fall in zone 9-11 gardens. All parts of the plant contain a milky, toxic sap that can irritate skin and eyes; wear gloves when pruning and keep away from children and pets. In zone 9, treat as a root-hardy perennial that dies back after frost and resprouts in spring; in zone 10-11 it remains evergreen.
